source: Who do you trust to help you unmask them?
The hourglass empties. The days have passed.
Less than one cock's crow remains.
I won't die this time. I'll find a way to stop it. I have to.
Godspeed, Ophelia.
I understand now why my son adores you so.
By the by, I've noticed you are free of your assassin, are you not? You have won this battle.
But not the war. Not so long as I'm still stuck in this world.
No. Not the war.
Quince told me something odd when I first had Brit arrested.
He said he had 'adjusted' the state of the world so that it would never happen again. Can he really do that?
Indeed, it appears he has already done so. See for yourself if he speaks true.
Though by what power he does these things, I know not.
Ah. Still living, I see. So you managed to stay your fate.
I'm impressed. But tomorrow, it will save you no more than the others.
More ominous warnings. Do you have anything else to offer me?
It's what the dead do best.
Fortinbras marches even now. Less than a day, Ophelia.
Can you save them from him?
Fortinbras is merely doing what conquerors do. But my family and friends...
They are tearing each other apart like men on patrol in a starving winter.
It shall not end until Elsinore lies silent.
Now. What news do you bring?
S-Spirit? Do you-- are you here?
Indeed. I am that body once called King Hamlet.
(It does look just like Hamlet's father.)
Do you remember me, my lord?
In vague silhouettes and shadows. Memory in death is a struggle. It is faint and infrequent.
I recall you were a young girl once. Such a rambunctious child. I knew you then.
Yes. You did.
There's something I need to confirm. You also experience time repeating?
In the graveyard, you told me to meet you here, now. But that was a different world.
Yes. A world now forever locked behind time's barrier.
You came to protect Gertrude.
The desire to see her safe is often the only thing powerful enough to rouse me.
But in this world, she does not even know of my existence. Would that she and I could speak alone just once.
I have only a single selfish request.
But it may be of use to you.
What is it, my lord?
Seek out your father. Watch what he does when he believes he is alone.
My notes—my notes, taken by him, out of love, out of protection—
They contain the terrifying details of my ordeal. Details I cannot recall. Things too hazy to remember fully.
But that ordeal is the reason I still linger, trapped here.
Find the notes, and there may be freedom for us both.
I have witnessed that your father keeps my possessions under most private lock and key.
The key is on his person at all times. Only he may access what is mine.
You're saying you don't remember any of this?
How can that be possible?
There are stronger forces than I at work. Even now, I can only hold my form for so long. Everything from before I walked these walls is... distant.
Find those pages. They rest in your father's care. Please.
Another one to ashes.
What's best for Her Majesty and for Hamlet.
With everything that's going on, precautions must be taken.
Stop—stop, Father!
Ophelia, you couldn't possibly understand. What these documents contained—
Burning these papers is a blessing to the one who wrote them.
Some day I hope you will understand the everlasting dedication I bear to this royal family. This is the depth of it.
If you tell His Majesty about this, it'll be my head.
Ah. My lady!
Lord Polonius. I've come to claim some property of mine.
Property, my lady?
Tell me, Polonius. When my husband died...
What was it, precisely, that my husband and I requested of all in Elsinore?
Ah. Yes, I recall.
You asked us all to turn over everything of King Hamlet's we owned, my lady. And I did.
Did you?
Or have you hidden something from me still?
W-well, my lady—I was trying to—
Preparing to destroy evidence of something, perhaps?
Please. My lady. I destroyed those things to protect him.
If there ever were such documents, they are long gone now.
I have destroyed nothing. I merely withheld these documents to protect him.
So you still have them in your possession?
So it's true? You—are saying—my husband left something you never showed us?
You lied to us. After I trusted you implicitly.
I regret that I have broken your trust.
A man has two deaths, they say.
Once when he dies, and once when his legacy is forgotten.
I served your husband Hamlet for all of his life. I didn't want anyone—you, least of all—to have to see the way he was, in the end.
You don't think I know how he was? How he looked at me with such pity and despair?
He was my husband, Polonius. Nothing he could have written in those notes could be so shameful as to be worth hiding.
I am sorry, my lady. It is done. The notes are burned, their contents ash.
Then there's nothing more to say to you.
I thought I could trust you.
All I have of him are the things he left behind, now.
And it seems even those are going to ash—one by one.
(So the notes have already been destroyed this time. I see. I'm too late.)
Give me those notes. Now.
I will not, my lady. I served—and still serve—King Hamlet above any other.
What do you think you're doing?
What I should have done the day he died.
I promised your late husband I would burn these, and I am not about to forego such a promise. I apologize sincerely, but I cannot hand these to you.
Right in front of me. The gall.
You feeble, old, doddering fool!
(Oh, my God. His head is in the flames.)
No! No...
But he crossed me. It was in defense. Defense of my husband, not my own life.
I—I had to do it.
You killed him.
I had no choice. I had no choice, Hamlet, my love. I swear it.
Oh, Hamlet, Hamlet, Hamlet!.
(She's not in her right mind.)
I must know. The price paid!
These notes--
This cannot be right. My husband didn't write this.
What does it say?
I-it isn't real, Ophelia, is it?
Tell me it isn't true. It cannot be.
T-these notes are pure madness! They make no sense! My husband, he suffered alone—
Just like my poor Hamlet.
I f-failed them both.
She left the notes sitting in that chest.
Though now, I'm worried about the Queen's state. Where did she run off to?
My King? W-What brings you here?
Evening, Polonius. I've come from a most fascinating conversation.
On what topic?
As I understand it, you have some personal writings my brother may have left behind.
Did I not ask upon his death that all of his remaining belongings be turned over to me, immediately?
You did.
I don't know what you speak of, my lord. I turned everything over. Truly.
Is it possible you have hidden something from me still?
That chest of yours. The one by the fire. Open it.
I cannot, my lord.
Open it, or spend an evening in a darkened cell as we take the keyring off your neck.
There. It is open.
And here you have its contents.
What is this?
Do you take me for an idiot?
This is a handful of ash!
It is all that remains.
You are too late to read his words, now. But I will never forget them.
I know what you did. I know who you truly are.
And your brother knew, too.
He wrote about it as a prophet might. He spoke of a poisoning. Of dying in the garden. And all of it came to pass.
This is certainly his handwriting.
What is this rambling nonsense?
This is—lunacy. Sheer lunacy. There's no sense in it!
He sounds like a raving madman. Half of this is indecipherable.
This is what my brother left behind?
Well, then. So be it. This is no threat to me.
Let the flames take it all.
Did anyone else read them?
Good. Then good riddance to that drivel.
Truth, you mean.
Some of that was fiction, certainly. But my lord Hamlet spoke of dying by your hand.
I do not believe that is a falsehood.
So my brother suspected me, did he? I can't imagine how!
Never was especially sharp in knowing what I felt about him.
I can hardly imagine what would have come from it, had my wife or nephew seen those notes.
What a blessing it is that we've spared them such pain.
I will always know the truth.
You may wear the crown, Claudius, but so long as you do, your brother will be my only King.
Hmm. Interesting.
Am I to understand, then, that you intended to use these notes to have me declared a murderer?
Originally, yes.
I held onto them for that purpose. I wanted to see you brought to justice.
But I have my daughter and son to think about. I have no interest in that now.
Why, I misjudged you, old fool. Seems age does come with wisdom.
Make no mistake. It would have ended very poorly for you. And for Ophelia, too.
I suggest you consider your next steps very carefully, my good Duke.
If ever your tongue starts to loosen, I want you to drink a glass of something stiff and imagine what your children's corpses might look like.
And then I want you to leave Elsinore. Permanently.
You're a monster, Claudius. But I've always known that.
So have I.
It is in my nature, sweet Ophelia. Don't begrudge me for it.
Good night, my lord, my lady.
We should all be grateful your daughter brought this to my attention.
I'm sorry you had to see this, Ophelia.
This is the ugly side of ruling. Sometimes one must take drastic measures to keep the peace.
Ophelia? What's going on? He hasn't threatened you, has he?
No, he hasn't. I'm fine, Father.
We'll be leaving. Until next time, Polonius.
Lord Hamlet?
You snake. What have you been hiding?
My lord. I don't understand.
My father died, and you were ordered to turn over anything of his belongings to my mother.
Why did you not obey?
W-well, my Prince, I w-was—I was trying to—
No. I destroyed those things to protect him.
You mean you've already destroyed them?
What could you possibly protect him from? Surely not death!
I apologize, my lord. But if such notes existed, they are long gone now.
What are you trying to hide, Polonius?
Give them to me at once!
This is something you cannot yet understand, my Prince.
I served your father for all of his life. I didn't want anyone—least of all you, or your mother—to have to see the way he was in the end.
You don't get to make that choice for us.
No. You don't get to take that away from me.
I am sorry, my lord. It is done. The notes are burned, their contents ash.
